connection: Production now uses interfaces for real variation. Forcing inheritance into those services would weaken the design, so this language comparison belongs in ScratchPad. Teach inheritance and abstract members in ScratchPad because TimeClock has no verified requirement for a class hierarchy.
objectives: Explain what HoursPolicyBase adds beyond what IHoursPolicy alone already provided: a shared, non-abstract Round helper both derived classes inherit for free.
Distinguish HoursPolicyBase's abstract GetVariance (each derived class must supply its own) from its concrete Round (shared, inherited, never overridden).
Confirm StandardHoursPolicy.GetVariance's override keyword is required, and explain what the compiler checks it against.
Preview why PayrollDbContext (Session 31) will be this codebase's first real, necessary use of inheritance -- EF Core requires a DbContext subclass, not just an interface implementation.

visuals.title: An abstract class can mix required and shared members
visuals.explanation: HoursPolicyBase declares GetVariance as abstract (each subclass must implement it) and Round as a concrete, shared protected method (subclasses inherit it unchanged).

visuals.title: override is checked against the abstract declaration
visuals.explanation: StandardHoursPolicy.GetVariance must use override, and its signature must match HoursPolicyBase's abstract declaration exactly, or the compiler rejects it.

visuals.title: Round is never duplicated
visuals.explanation: Neither StandardHoursPolicy nor FlexibleHoursPolicy defines its own Round method -- both inherit the single implementation from HoursPolicyBase.

visuals.title: An interface alone could not have done this
visuals.explanation: IHoursPolicy could declare GetVariance, but interfaces (before default interface members) cannot supply Round's shared implementation the way an abstract base class can.

preQuiz.prompt: Why is this lesson in ScratchPad?
options: TimeClock has no verified class-hierarchy requirement
preQuiz.explanation: Do not invent a hierarchy for the product.

preQuiz.prompt: Can an abstract class be instantiated directly?
preQuiz.explanation: It is an incomplete base for derived types.

preQuiz.prompt: What must a concrete derived class do with an abstract member?
preQuiz.explanation: The override supplies the missing implementation.

concept.title: Abstract classes combine requirements and shared code
paragraphs: An abstract member requires each derived type to provide behavior. A concrete member supplies shared behavior once.
ScratchPad is appropriate because TimeClock's production variation is already modeled naturally with interfaces.

concept.title: Derived types override required behavior
paragraphs: A derived class uses override to fulfill the abstract contract. It inherits concrete members without copying them.
The hierarchy should represent a genuine is-a relationship, not a desire to reuse a few lines.

concept.title: Interfaces and abstract classes solve different problems
paragraphs: Interfaces describe capabilities across otherwise unrelated implementations. Abstract classes model a related family that benefits from shared implementation.
The production repository boundary needs substitution, not a shared base implementation, so it remains interface-based.

steps: Define one small abstract base type with one abstract and one concrete member.

postQuiz.prompt: When is an abstract class a good fit?
options: For a related family with shared implementation
postQuiz.explanation: Both relationship and shared behavior should be meaningful.

options: They need substitutable capabilities, not inherited implementation
postQuiz.explanation: The design pressure is substitution across storage implementations.

postQuiz.prompt: What happens to the concrete helper on a derived class?

reflections: Why did this course choose to add a new abstract class (HoursPolicyBase) rather than leave Session 19 without any real inheritance example at all?
What would you lose if HoursPolicyBase's Round method were duplicated separately inside StandardHoursPolicy and FlexibleHoursPolicy instead of shared?
Now that you've seen both an interface-only design (Session 18's original IHoursPolicy) and an abstract-class design (this session's HoursPolicyBase), when would you reach for each?
whatBreaks: Attempting new HoursPolicyBase() directly fails to compile, because abstract classes exist only to be extended, never instantiated on their own. Removing StandardHoursPolicy's override keyword from GetVariance produces a compile error, because the compiler can no longer connect that method to HoursPolicyBase's abstract declaration. Duplicating Round's logic separately inside each derived policy (instead of inheriting it) would reintroduce the exact kind of duplication generics (Session 14) and interfaces (Session 18) already exist to avoid.
summary: HoursPolicyBase is a new, clearly-labeled abstract class -- nothing in the production code uses inheritance, so this session builds one specifically to demonstrate what an abstract class adds beyond an interface: a required abstract member (GetVariance) alongside a shared, concrete, inherited one (Round). Session 31's PayrollDbContext will be this codebase's first genuinely framework-required use of inheritance, previewed here so it does not feel unmotivated when it arrives.
